reclamation.why: Technically still exercisable but practically worthless, so not relied on. Under 11 U.S.C. Sec. 546(c)(1) (library: bc_503b9_546c.md), goods received within 45 days pre-petition (on/after 2026-01-24: MS-7740, MS-7788, MS-7815) may be reclaimed only by written demand not later than 45 days after receipt or 20 days after the petition (2026-03-30) where the 45 days expire post-commencement; no such written reclamation demand has been made (the 2026-03-12 letter was an automated payment-demand, not a demand for return of goods). All three shipments' demand windows converge on 2026-03-30: 45 days after each receipt (2026-02-04 -> 2026-03-21; 2026-02-20 -> 2026-04-06; 2026-03-04 -> 2026-04-18) would all expire post-commencement, so the statute's 20-days-after-petition date (2026-03-30) governs every one of them. Decisively, the library states reclamation is subject to prior liens - here the DIP lender's blanket lien - so reclamation would recover nothing. The same MS-7788/MS-7815 goods are already captured by the Sec. 503(b)(9) administrative claim, which is the effective route. Client gave no go/no-go and no facts on goods identifiability; default recommendation is NO-GO (no spend). Assumption: Mesa holds no purchase-money security interest.

ordinary_course_defense.reasoning: Petition 2026-03-10; 90-day window opens 2025-12-10 (11 U.S.C. Sec. 547(b)(4), (f); library: bc_547.md). Four payments fall inside: 2025-12-18 $51,000 (45 days after invoice, ACH), 2026-01-22 $44,000 (43 days, ACH), 2026-02-10 $48,200 (29 days, ACH), 2026-02-27 $36,800 (25 days, WIRE demanded by Mesa). Protected (Sec. 547(c)(2)(A)): the 12/18 and 1/22 payments (=$95,000) match the parties' 12-month history of 43-47 day ACH payments on a regular cadence. Exposed (= $85,000): the 2/10 payment (29 days - well outside the 43-47 day history, arriving after Mesa's unilateral 2026-01-20 shortening of terms to NET 15, and the library states payments under shortened terms generally fall outside (c)(2)(A)) and the 2/27 partial payment (25 days, wire on demand - the library expressly names 'wire on demand' under 'pressure' as outside (c)(2)(A)). Sec. 547(c)(2)(B) (ordinary industry terms) could protect the 2/10 payment, but the client has NO industry payment-terms evidence, so this fallback is currently unsupported - flagged open. Burden on these defenses is Mesa's (Sec. 547(g)).

stay_violations: 2026-03-12: 'FINAL NOTICE - pay $210,000 within 5 days or we refer to collections' letter, mailed and emailed 2 days post-petition - an act to collect a pre-petition claim, 11 U.S.C. Sec. 362(a)(6) (library: bc_362.md: 'Dunning letters ... after the petition are acts to collect'). Client states this was generated by an AUTOMATED notice program triggered at 30 days late. Automation does not cure the violation, and the program is presumed STILL RUNNING against Redwood: every further automated letter/email is a fresh violation and the automation pattern is strong evidence of willfulness once Mesa knew of the case. Remedy note: Sec. 362(k) by its text compensates 'an individual injured' by a willful violation; Redwood is a corporation, so its route is Sec. 105 sanctions - the library states courts also sanction corporate debtors' creditors for willful violations under Sec. 105.

2026-03-15: collection call to Redwood AP demanding payment, made after Redwood told the caller it had filed Chapter 11 - a collection call post-petition, Sec. 362(a)(6). Client (Frank) adds that 'Lori' called twice - the dunning log documents only the one 3/15 call, so at least one call is undocumented; dates/content unknown and must be pinned down for any stay-violation response (sanctions exposure runs through Sec. 105 because Redwood is a corporation; Sec. 362(k) by its text covers individual debtors). Being told of the filing on 3/15 fixes knowledge for everything after.

2026-03-18: email to Redwood CFO threatening to 'hold all future shipments and report to credit bureaus' - sent after Mesa knew of the petition; the credit-bureau threat is expressly an act to collect per the library, Sec. 362(a)(6). Its post-knowledge timing makes willfulness very hard to contest. Because Redwood is a corporation, the exposure is Sec. 105 sanctions per the library, not Sec. 362(k) damages - (k) by its text runs to 'an individual injured.'
